tagline: Red-rock buttes frame the northbound approach through the Village of Oak Creek to Sedona.
intro: The Red Rock Scenic Byway winds through Sedona’s high-desert red-rock country. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as a 7.5-mile All-American Road and gives twenty minutes for the drive, with several hours for activities. Its description emphasizes the diversity of the high desert; Wikipedia records the 2006 designation as recognition of the red rock and sandstone formations along the road. Along the route, the Village of Oak Creek occupies an open area among red-rock buttes and canyons, surrounded by Coconino National Forest.

The number SR 179 first belonged to a different route, designated between 1935 and 1939 from SR 79 to SR 69 in Prescott Valley. By 1960, that route had been canceled and the number assigned to the present road.

From I-17’s exit 298, SR 179 heads briefly northwest, then curves north toward the Village of Oak Creek. Bell Rock’s scenic area adjoins the village’s north end. Entering Sedona, the highway follows Oak Creek’s east bank and crosses the creek before ending at SR 89A.
notice: Bell Rock’s sedimentary layers lie in horizontal beds.

moments.title: Bell Rock
moments.text: Bell Rock rises just north of the Village of Oak Creek, with Courthouse Butte immediately to its east. Horizontal beds of sedimentary rock make up the butte. The hiking route described in Wikipedia reaches a small plateau on the northwest face. That plateau is below the summit: reaching the top requires a challenging, unmarked trail.

moments.title: Cathedral Rock
moments.text: Cathedral Rock’s name has not always matched the map. Some early maps labeled it Court House Rock, while the separate Courthouse Butte appeared as Church House Rock. The sandstone butte stands about one mile west of SR 179 in Coconino National Forest. A short, steep trail from Back O’ Beyond reaches the gaps between its rock formations. Ripple marks are visible along the lower trail, and a black basalt dike can be seen in the first saddle. The summit reaches 4,967 feet above sea level, while the described hiking route ends at the saddle points.

moments.title: Chapel of the Holy Cross
moments.text: A cross is both symbol and structure at the Chapel of the Holy Cross. Local rancher and sculptor Marguerite Brunswig Staude commissioned the chapel, built into Sedona’s red-rock buttes between 1954 and 1956. August K. Strotz designed it, with Richard Hein as project architect. Workers moved upwards of 25 tons of rock without dynamite. The walls were sandblasted inside and out to expose their textured aggregate, and gray glass reduces glare at the two ends. The approach continues the concrete work: a long, curved ramp of textured concrete leads from the parking area to the chapel.
